newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Benetton 1996 net profit up, cash mounts.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Benetton 1996 net profit up, cash mounts.

text.p: Italian clothing group Benetton boosted its 1996 net profit 11.5 percent and said on Thursday it intended to raise its dividend by 18 percent.
Analysts said the results were fairly in line with forecasts but they foresaw a slowdown in net profit growth in 1997.
The main question mark remained on what the group intended to do with a 133 billion lire ($80 million) cash pile.

"Benetton is a very efficient company and well managed and because of that there are no surprises. It's a mature business but with no huge upside," said one analyst at a UK investment house who declined to be named.
"On the balance sheet side they have got a substantial net cash position even though they are increasing the dividend, which means that an acquisition is very likely," he said.
Benetton's consolidated net profit rose to a record 246 billion lire from 220 billion in 1995 and it said it would pay a dividend on ordinary shares of 500 lire, up from 425 previously.
The group ended the year with liquidity of 133 billion lire compared with net debt of 140 billion at the end of 1995.
"Net debt has been cleared for the first time in the history of the group," it said.

Turnover was 2.87 trillion lire, down from 2.94 trillion in 1995. The group noted the effect of marked appreciation of the lira against major currencies and pointed out it had also sold off some non-strategic operations.
Its operating result was 401.7 billion against 443.8 billion previously while the gross operating margin fell to 1.15 trillion from 1.22 billion.
Sales around the globe had grown four percent with steady growth in European markets and the Middle East.

Paul Gordon at IMI-Sigeco investment house here said the increase in the dividend was satisfying for investors as an even-handed way of giving something back to minority shareholders rather than simply to the Benetton family.
But questions still hung over what the company would do with the cash pile.
Even if it jacked the dividend higher still, "the likelihood is that in the next few years they will be generating more cash than they can use," Gordon said.
Benetton managing director Carlo Gilardi told Reuters last month the cash must have a return but an acquisition would be made only if that purchase had the same prospects as Benetton.

Gordon said it would be hard to graft another operation on to the Benetton system of manufacturing, commissioned agents and licensed retail outlets. "The Benetton system is a unique system and trying to attach something to it is difficult," he said.

Sports equipment company Benetton Sportsystem, which is owned by the Benetton family's Edizione Holding, had been pondered as a possibility. Even though there was no progress on this front, it still could not be ruled out, Gordon said.
As far as 1997 was concerned, analysts said the group was likely to see net profits grow at a slower pace than in 1996.

"In 1997 I expect them to make more or less the same -- maybe two to three percent more in terms of sales...and with a net profit of a maximum five to six percent higher," the British investment house analyst said.
Gordon said he expected operating profit growth of around 10 percent "but most of that will get lost once we get to the net profit because we won't get a foreign exchange effect."
As a result he expected there would be little progress on net profits in 1997 because of continuing lira strength.
